html:
Unique Research · Insight · April 19, 2024

Author: Dan Ge (葛泳麟), Lion City Capital (狮城资本). MarTech as a more must-have enterprise revenue tool than pure cost-cut/admin software has long been the digital-upgrade spearhead — the largest share of the U.S. Cloud100 and a unicorn factory. Yet with slower growth and rising traffic costs, China MarTech penetration remains low. Beyond U.S.–China software-environment differences, the author argues most enterprises still apply traditional software thinking to cost-down/efficiency — and people in China are not that expensive, so value is limited. To win in China, MarTech should center on revenue growth. This piece sketches breakout directions from marketing environment, industry challenges, international lessons, and primary-market status.

Core China challenges from U.S.–China differences

Aside from industrial soil advantages, China’s MarTech core disadvantage is the marketing environment — especially closed data ecosystems and extremely complex, fast-changing reach:

  1. Data fragmentation, closed ecosystems. Domestic giants/social platforms treat data as monopoly assets with very low openness (not a tech problem) — hard to close loops. Overseas (Facebook, Google) largely sandbox-open data so SaaS vendors do ETL and matching, then share media spend — giving MarTech huge room. Domestically, coarse crowd tags / first-party data dominate; a large share of MarTech entry is the data layer — building own DBs or private domains as digital marketing’s first station — often decoupled from marketing outcomes in execution.
  2. Marketing media / user behavior iterates too fast. Reach channels are far more complex than the U.S., especially WeChat ecosystem (Moments / mini programs / official accounts / e-commerce / livestream / Channels…). Full-touchpoint tools are required at higher bar. Unlike ERP/finance/HR (relatively stable best practices), marketing is about reading external customer behavior — especially B2C — with huge variables and destructive innovation (audiences, habits, media, tech). Products/services are inherently non-standard and operationally unstable.

From the customer view, value priority is always RoI conversion first, then process assetization / automated operating standards. Marketing is a fast-iterating, data-driven cognition industry; traditional software thinking hits a ceiling in China MarTech.

MarTech giants’ development history

HubSpot, Adobe, and Salesforce all grew from initial product DNA, chose the right strategic path, then merged toward today’s all-in-one marketing stacks. Most instructive for MarTech: HubSpot (marketing-cloud DNA).

HubSpot

Core entry via marketing cloud (Marketing Hub from 2006; largest revenue share). Two decisive strategies:

  1. Inbound / content marketing orientation (pull). HubSpot pioneered Inbound — attract via quality content, build trust, convert. HubSpot itself is the model: massive Blog/Twitter/Facebook/LinkedIn attention; multi-year SEO + social ops; lead capture. New users: 33% word-of-mouth, 26% SEO/Google, 13% HubSpot’s own blog. Customer growth (45%) outpaced revenue growth (40%).
  2. Powerful partner ecosystem. 1,300+ third-party apps on the partner platform; HubSpot also API-accessible. Partners use HubSpot tools to serve clients; HubSpot amplifies partners — win-win. Ecosystem expands customers and reputation; partners shift project→subscription cash flow; partner sales get ~20% commission. ~40% of revenue from ecosystem partners → sales expense ratio ~50%.

Both strategies answer traditional outbound (push) pain:

  • Outbound has too many variables (media, brand tone, consumer behavior); as markets mature, push marketing grows less effective — high-quality conversion hard to sustain (hence many U.S. long-tail outbound MarTech firms survive; not winner-take-all).
  • Outbound is short-term sales–heavy; Inbound builds long-term trust and brand stickiness.
  • Higher RoI: Inbound via digital channels (social, SEO) often costs less.

HubSpot’s long-term strategy — inbound + massive partners, adapting to change and reaching the long tail — is its success core.

Adobe & Salesforce (different DNA)

Adobe started with 2C creative tools (Creative Cloud). Core strategy: occupy absolute mindshare among content designers (SaaS subscription reform; sky-high Figma acquisition — classic winner-takes-all), then M&A along the chain into marketing cloud (Ad Cloud + Analytics Cloud + Marketing Cloud).

Salesforce started with CRM (sales automation) — process-optimization DNA; heavy customization and homogenization are biggest challenges. After PaaS build years (2005–10 heavy spend) and years of product M&A, it connected full customer journeys (marketing–sales–service), raising stickiness and switching costs via a tightly linked product matrix. Both successes had historical contingency — hard to copy.

Because outbound is so complex, almost no enterprise vendor ships a complete closed-loop product alone. International giants took decades of M&A to assemble full matrices.

China MarTech status

Most MarTech firms still sell single-point solutions. Entry points roughly: system layer, data layer, ops layer — all still orbiting IT process cost-down/efficiency. Three common challenges:

  1. Homogenized competition. Marketing cloud still largely experience + IT–driven; tech barriers low; homogenization inevitable.
  2. Decoupled from outcomes. Business understanding and ops experience often stuck in limited first-party tags and subjective experience — hard to differentiate final conversion/media results. Future MarTech (esp. B2C private-domain) PK core metric is RoI — who productizes experience and analytics into intelligent decision layers tied to global RoI will decide willingness to pay.
  3. No closed-loop / all-in-one product. Large enterprises often buy several products that do not interconnect. Integrated delivery that strings modules into automation apps will be a hard need.

Winner pattern — three capabilities for the moat

Future China MarTech unicorns will likely build moats around three capabilities:

  1. Embrace AIGC; focus on content. Markets only get more mature and competitive; Inbound’s edge vs Outbound will grow clearer — and Inbound’s core methods (SEO, media strategy, content strategy, brand story) are easier to accumulate than Outbound’s many B2C variables. With GenAI: text→image/video/poster to raise content throughput, cut production cost, lower content-ops hiring bar, shorten cycles; simulation data for mock media prediction / sim A/B for content strategy. Creative GenAI is still early — designer cost-down ~30–80% depending on IT skill. We favor vendors with data accumulation + closed-loop link who can efficiently mass-produce high-end creative.
  2. RoI orientation — data decision capability is critical. MarTech centers on optimizing conversion and resource allocation across AIPL nodes. What directly decides marketing RoI is intelligent decisioning from consumer insight (data→precise media/spend strategy). This is the hardest, scarcest link — few founding teams have deep ops experience. Productizing ops experience, user insight, and industry understanding into a one-stop intelligent-decision marketing cloud will fundamentally help enterprises grow revenue (cf. Salesforce’s Einstein for B2B expert decisioning, then ~10 AI acquisitions to iterate; similar breakthroughs appear in China) — and outcompete tools that only chase cost-down/efficiency.
  3. M&A / ecosystem integration capability. MarTech is long-tail: global MarTech firm count grew ~65× from 2011–2022, still rising through COVID — because touchpoints change fast, knowledge iterates, cloud lowers entry barriers; overseas many excellent firms lead single points / new tech and coexist with giants (HubSpot ecosystem). In China ecosystems are immature; KA count, budgets, and willingness to pay only support head vendors — we expect a relatively concentrated landscape. Product/team DNA has biases and natural gaps; breakthrough via M&A or ecosystem building will be necessary. As China moves from competition to consolidation, we favor head firms with fast integration capability.

About Lion City Capital: see CN package for firm intro; charts/images (4) attach on ingest.

— END —
